notes: For non-emergency individual-patient use, a new IND ordinarily becomes effective 30 calendar days after FDA receipt unless held or FDA permits earlier use. An individual-patient protocol under an existing active IND has no automatic 30-day wait, but must be submitted and have applicable IRB approval and consent. Widespread-use treatment protocols have different start rules.

Emergency individual-patient use can receive prior FDA authorisation by telephone or other rapid communication, allowing use to begin before the written expanded-access submission. That submission is due within 15 working days of FDA authorisation. When there is insufficient time for prospective institutional review board (IRB) review, report the emergency use to the IRB within 5 working days of starting treatment. Subsequent use at the same institution normally requires prior IRB review. FDA's April 2026 guidance also describes discretion for a subsequent emergency request when prior review is infeasible, with the same 5-working-day reporting requirement. This is not continuing permission or a promised treatment date.

A licensed physician acting as sponsor-investigator can use Form FDA 3926 for an individual-patient expanded-access IND in a non-emergency or emergency setting. Forms FDA 1571 and 1572 remain an alternative. FDA also lists eRequest for non-emergency individual-patient requests. The streamlined form is not a marketing application, a form for group requests or the device-access process.

When an application references another sponsor’s IND, a letter of authorization permits FDA to reference specified product information. That permission does not itself authorize treatment or guarantee drug supply. If such a letter is unavailable, the FDA review division can advise which other information may satisfy the applicable requirements.

For an unapproved investigational drug supplied under an IND, the IND sponsor needs separate prior written FDA authorization to charge for the drug. Recoverable costs and other conditions differ between clinical trials and expanded access. Treatment authorization does not itself authorize charging, and permission to recover drug costs does not decide insurer payment or the total cost of clinical care.

A reported FDA authorization rate needs its stated submitted-request denominator, period and request categories. It does not measure the fraction of everyone seeking the drug who obtains manufacturer supply, meets every requirement or actually receives treatment. An application authorization is not a personal probability of access or benefit.

For individual-patient expanded access, authorised drug-cost recovery is limited to direct costs attributable specifically to supplying the drug for that authorised investigational use. Examples include per-unit manufacture or acquisition, shipping and storage. Commercial-scale facilities and equipment, and research, administrative or labour expenses that would occur anyway, are indirect costs excluded by 21 CFR 312.8(d)(1). This concerns the sponsor's authorised drug charge, not every bill for clinical care.

For intermediate-size populations and treatment INDs or protocols under 21 CFR 312.315 and 312.320, the regulation additionally permits specified monitoring, IND reporting and directly associated administrative costs. Those additional categories do not apply automatically to an individual-patient arrangement. FDA authorisation of the treatment and prior written permission to charge remain separate.

FDA's request-forms page reports that, on average, 99% of expanded-access requests may proceed. That is the page's submitted-request statement, without a period specified there, not the fraction of everyone seeking a drug who receives it or benefits. Manufacturer agreement is an independent supply gate, and Project Facilitate is an FDA oncology point of contact that helps clinicians navigate requests. The reported FDA fraction does not measure how often supply is the limiting step or rank the obstacles in a particular plan.

The charging calculation required by 21 CFR 312.8(d)(3) must have supporting documentation and a statement that an independent certified public accountant reviewed and approved it. Expanded-access permission to charge normally lasts one year from FDA authorisation, or less if FDA specifies; the sponsor can request reauthorisation. FDA must withdraw permission if charging interferes with development or its authorisation criteria cease to be met. A two-year-old letter therefore needs a current reauthorisation check. These rules concern the investigational drug charge, not a promise of free clinical care.

Build a readiness record around the actual product, formulation, dose, route and schedule, its clinical rationale and alternatives, and the supporting quality, exposure and safety information. Name the sponsor and treating clinician, supplier and receiving or storage team, administering service, urgent-care destination, and people responsible for response assessment, toxicity management and reporting. Record the applicable submissions, review and consent, usable supply, costs, dependencies and possible stop conditions. Mark each answer confirmed, proposed or unknown with its responsible person and date; a checklist does not determine a patient's status. The treating team must assess suitability before administration; a laboratory result supplies neither eligibility nor a safe regimen. This checklist concerns U.S. drugs and biologics; device access, other countries and institutional rules can differ.

In a fictional request, a supplier says manufacture could finish next week while institutional review, the treatment plan and monitoring remain unresolved. That is a manufacturing estimate, not a treatment date. Similarly, FDA permission without a service able to administer and monitor the product leaves a delivery gate open. Ask which milestones are complete and which depend on others. A fictional new non-emergency individual-patient IND with supplier agreement, the necessary product information, applicable IRB review and consent can proceed when effective, ordinarily 30 days after FDA receipt or earlier FDA notice, provided it is not on hold. Supplier review, manufacture, FDA review, institutional review, shipping and scheduling each need their own estimate and dependencies.

For non-emergency individual-patient use, a physician using Form FDA 3926 may request the permitted institutional review board (IRB) chairperson or designated-member concurrence procedure instead of review at a convened full-board meeting. Concurrence must precede treatment under that procedure. It is not a waiver of informed consent: obtain the applicable written consent on an IRB-approved form. The supplier's letter of authorisation lets FDA reference specified information and does not replace these steps or FDA permission to proceed.

records.name: Referral and eligibility assessment for CAR T-cell therapy
records.tldr: CAR T-cell therapy is given at specialist centres, and a team there decides. For large B-cell lymphoma that does not respond to first treatment or returns within a year, CAR T cells are now the standard next step, so early referral matters. The centre checks your fitness, heart, brain and blood, and you will need to stay near the hospital, with someone to help, for at least two weeks after.
records.summary:
EBMT 2025 indications (Table 1, adults; category/evidence level as printed): in large B-cell lymphoma, CAR T cells are standard of care (S/I) for primary refractory disease, early relapse with untested or chemoresistant disease and early chemosensitive relapse, where axicabtagene ciloleucel or lisocabtagene maraleucel beat salvage chemotherapy and autologous transplant in two phase III trials; for late relapse autologous transplant remains standard (S/II) and CAR T a clinical option (CO/II); after a failed autograft CAR T is standard (S/II). Follicular lymphoma: CAR T within the EMA labels, standard for refractory relapse (S/II). Mantle cell lymphoma: not first line outside trials; a clinical option second line after primary BTK inhibitor failure. Myeloma: idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel within their labels. Primary CNS lymphoma relapse: clinical option. Hodgkin lymphoma: not convincingly better than other options to date.

EBMT/JACIE 2019: the decision is made by a multidisciplinary team in a designated centre; cumulative chemotherapy harms T-cell quality, so plan collection early. SITC 2020: prior allogeneic transplant, BiTE or antibody therapy is no bar if the target antigen is expressed (LE: 4); weigh ECOG performance status; recent or active intracranial haemorrhage excludes (LE: 4); refer for neurological review if there is inflammatory neurological disease or CNS involvement; baseline CRP, ferritin, LDH, blood count, chemistry and echocardiogram or MUGA (LE: 4). FDA 2025: the REMS ended; labels now ask patients to stay near a healthcare facility for at least two weeks and not to drive for two weeks.
records.simple: A specialist team decides whether CAR T-cell therapy is right for you. If it is, you will need to stay close to the hospital, with a helper, for at least two weeks afterwards.
records.population: Adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell lymphoma, B-cell ALL or multiple myeloma, and children and young adults with B-cell ALL, being considered for a licensed CAR T-cell product. Indications and reimbursement differ by country; the EBMT categories are European. CAR T cells for autoimmune disease and solid tumours are outside this protocol.
records.trigger: Relapse or refractoriness in a disease for which a CAR T-cell product is licensed, or a referring team asking whether a patient is a candidate.

steps.action: Refer to a designated CAR T-cell centre, where the decision is made by its multidisciplinary team
steps.why: The treatment and its side effects need a specialist team and hospital set up for them.
steps.quote: The decision to treat a patient with CAR T cells therapy should be made collectively at a multidisciplinary team meeting in a designated center for CAR T-cell therapy.

steps.action: For large B-cell lymphoma that is primary refractory or relapses early, refer for second-line CAR T-cell therapy
steps.why: In two phase III trials CAR T cells kept the lymphoma controlled for longer than chemotherapy and transplant in this group.
steps.quote: For patients with primary refractory disease or early relapse with untested or chemorefractory disease, treatment with axi-cel or liso-cel represents the current standard of care.

steps.action: For late relapse of large B-cell lymphoma, consider autologous transplant first, with CAR T cells after a failed transplant
steps.why: Autologous transplant still works well for late relapse and has not been beaten in a trial.
steps.quote: Patients with late relapses face reasonable outcomes with auto-HCT and this standard has not been challenged by a clinical trial as of today.

steps.action: In mantle cell lymphoma, do not use CAR T cells first line outside trials; consider them second line after BTK inhibitor failure
steps.why: The licence and the evidence are for disease that has failed earlier treatment.
steps.quote: With Bruton’s TKIs moving to 1st-line treatment, CAR-T has become a clinical option as 2nd-line therapy in patients with primary Bruton’s TKIs failure.

steps.action: Refer early, before further lines of chemotherapy where possible
steps.why: Each course of chemotherapy weakens the T cells from which the product is made.
steps.quote: There is evidence that cumulative chemotherapy exposure adversely affects the quality of circulating T cells.

steps.action: Do not exclude a patient for earlier allogeneic transplant, bispecific T-cell engager or antibody therapy if the cancer still expresses the target
steps.why: These do not stop CAR T cells working if the target is still present.
steps.quote: Patients who have previously undergone allo-HSCT, bispecific T cell engager (BiTE) therapy, anti-CD19 monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapy, and mAbs against other targets (eg, rituximab) may be treated with CAR T cells, provided the patient’s disease still expresses the target antigen

steps.action: Assess performance status, and do not proceed with recent or active bleeding in the brain
steps.why: Side effects can be severe; a recent brain bleed makes neurotoxicity especially dangerous.
steps.quote: Patients with evidence of recent or active intracranial hemorrhage should not undergo CAR T cell therapy

steps.action: Refer for neurological review if there is inflammatory neurological disease or lymphoma in the brain or spinal cord
steps.why: Existing brain disease changes the risk and the monitoring plan for neurotoxicity.
steps.quote: Patients with history of inflammatory neurological conditions or current CNS disease involvement should be referred for additional neurological consultation prior to initiating CAR T cell therapy.

steps.action: Take baseline CRP, ferritin, LDH, blood count, kidney, liver and mineral chemistry, and an echocardiogram or MUGA scan
steps.why: Baselines make it possible to recognise toxicity early, and heart function must be adequate.
steps.quote: Prior to CAR T cell therapy, treating physicians should order CRP, ferritin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), complete blood counts, comprehensive metabolic panel (including Mg/Pho), and transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) or multigated acquisition (MUGA) scan.

steps.action: Plan for the patient to stay near a healthcare facility for at least two weeks after infusion, and not to drive for two weeks
steps.why: Cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity usually start in the first two weeks and can come on fast.
steps.quote: Specifically, labeling update included revision to language to monitor patients for at least two weeks including daily monitoring for at least one week; to instruct patients to remain within proximity of a healthcare facility for at least two weeks; and to advise patients to avoid driving for two weeks following product administration

bestInClass.statement: For who should be referred, the EBMT 2025 indications are the most recent guideline read in full: CAR T cells are standard of care (S/I) for large B-cell lymphoma that is primary refractory or relapses early, on the strength of two randomised phase III trials, and the standard after a failed autograft (S/II); autologous transplant stays standard for late relapse (S/II). For the eligibility work-up, SITC 2020 (LE: 4) and EBMT/JACIE 2019 (ungraded) agree on a specialist multidisciplinary decision, performance status, baseline inflammatory markers and cardiac function, and neurological assessment. EBMT 2025 and its retrospective evidence leave one open point: for early chemosensitive relapse that reaches complete remission on salvage, EBMT rates CAR T S/I but also calls autologous transplant a valid clinical option (CO/II). In the US the FDA ended the REMS in June 2025 and relaxed proximity and driving restrictions to two weeks; European labels were not read.

variants.name: Autologous transplant for early chemosensitive relapse in complete remission (EBMT 2025)
variants.differs: For large B-cell lymphoma relapsing early but reaching complete remission on salvage, consolidates with high-dose therapy and autologous transplant rather than CAR T cells.
variants.evidence: Rated CO/II; a retrospective analysis found better progression-free survival with autologous transplant than CAR T in this group, but included no second-line CAR T and mostly tisagenlecleucel.

variants.name: US monitoring after the REMS (FDA 2025)
variants.differs: Removes the requirement for specially certified hospitals with immediate on-site tocilizumab; labels require monitoring for at least two weeks with daily monitoring for at least one, proximity for two weeks and no driving for two weeks.
variants.evidence: Regulatory decision based on established management guidelines and stable adverse event reporting.
